title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (3 of 7)
hook: a text about letting go that tells you to live a hundred years, working
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tyaktena: by that renounced, enjoy. Do not covet; whose is wealth? Your line: let them go when they go.

Why not just quit? If everything belongs to the Lord, and the wise thing is to let go, why not leave the job, leave the inbox, and go sit under a tree? Some in the tradition have done exactly that, and they're honored for it. But the very next verse of the Isha says something closer to the opposite. It's the verse that makes this tiny Upanishad a favorite of people with rent to pay.
screen: `WHY NOT JUST QUIT?` → `THE NEXT VERSE.` → `NOT THE ANSWER YOU EXPECT.`

segments.voice: Verse two: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah. Doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years. Karmani is works, actions, the same karma you learned on day seven: action, and what it grows. Shatam samah, a hundred years, is the full human life in the old Vedic hope. So the text that just said let go now says: live long, and keep working. Then the reason. For you, living this way, there is no other way; action does not cling to a person. The word for cling pictures something smeared on, like oil or mud. Actions done in the spirit of verse one, knowing all this belongs to the Lord, don't glue themselves to you. That's the seed of the Gita's karma yoga, which you spent weeks with: act fully, and don't cling to the fruit. Here it is centuries earlier, in two lines. Verse three is darker. It speaks of worlds called asurya, covered in blind darkness, where those who are killers of the self go. Some translators hear asurya as sunless; others, Shankara among them, as the worlds of the asuras. Either way, it's dark. Most commentators don't read killers of the self as literal suicide, but as people who live as if the self weren't there at all, burying the light under grabbing. So the three verses stack up. All this is the Lord's. Enjoy it by letting go. And keep working, a hundred years if you get them, without letting the work stick. Renounce, and enjoy, and get up tomorrow.
screen: `DOING WORKS HERE.` · `LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `ACTION DOES NOT CLING.` · `THE WORLDS OF BLIND DARKNESS.` · then, large: `RENOUNCE, AND KEEP WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary task waiting for you, a report, the dishes, a phone call, and see yourself doing it well, then finishing it and letting it go, the way you'd wash oil off your hands. Breathe in as you picture the work; breathe out as you picture it done and released. If your mind runs to the result, how it'll be judged, notice that, and come back to the doing.
Karma, action, works. Verse two adds: and keep working. Doing works here, wish to live a hundred years; action done this way doesn't cling.
Your line: don't let the work stick. Work done this way doesn't follow you to dinner. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Isha verse 2 to show that the Upanishads do not require leaving the world: a householder can work a full life without being bound by the work.

fork.setup: you've understood that all this belongs to the Lord. what does verse two tell you to do next?
options: stop acting, since nothing is yours.
keep doing your work, a hundred years if you get them.
act only for what you'll gain.
fork.reveal: keep working. done this way, the text says, action does not cling to you.

original.note: Sanskrit: karma, action; verse two uses karmani, works, from the root kri, to do.

trapdoor: what you thought: letting go means dropping out.
what it means: the Isha says keep working, and let the work not stick to you.
what a scholar hears: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah; the verb for cling (lip) means to smear, as with oil.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 2 (doing works, live a hundred years; action does not cling)

notes: Verse 2's 'na karma lipyate nare': the cling verb as 'smear' (lip) — check.
Verse 3 'atmahano': reading as those who ignore the self, not literal suicide — check commentators (Shankara reads it as those ignorant of the self).
Claim that the Isha predates the Gita: consensus dating, but phrase 'centuries earlier' should be checked.

Audit (second sample): the teach glossed asurya flatly as 'sunless'. The word as usually printed (asuryā) is read by Shankara and many translators as 'of the asuras', and 'sunless' (a-sūrya) is a second, popular reading; the teach now gives both, and the match pair no longer asserts 'sunless'. The teach screen head now reads THE WORLDS OF BLIND DARKNESS.
